solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ruined health on diet eating duck dish

indicators.note: ruined letters are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order
the anagram swallows the duck, holding it inside

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: Someone whose health has been wrecked by a diet that includes a duck dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged twelve letters take in O, so all thirteen are mixed together. Toad-in-the-hole is a British dish of sausages baked in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: Toad-in-the-hole is a traditional British dish of sausages cooked in Yorkshire pudding batter.

clue.text: Branch manager Greene tours abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean scattered widely, so the letters are spread out and rearranged

explanation.surface: A bank's branch manager called Greene travelling on overseas tours.
explanation.walkthrough: "Branch manager" reads as a bank job, and Greene looks like a novelist's name; the branches are on trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree surgeon looks after trees, cutting and managing their branches.

clue.text: Pervasive quality of first-class travellers

blocks.note: A is the top grade, as in A1
the Roma are a travelling people

explanation.surface: A remark about the all-pervading atmosphere among people travelling first class.
explanation.walkthrough: "First-class travellers" looks like one phrase about train passengers; it splits into A and ROMA.
explanation.definitionFit: An aroma is a distinctive quality that pervades something, as in an aroma of scandal.

clue.text: What you do in pub close to crapulent bankrupt

indicators.note: one thing sits in another
the close of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: what you, the solver, do to this clue

explanation.surface: What a drunken regular gets up to in the pub before going broke.
explanation.walkthrough: IN(SOLVE)N then T. "What you do" addresses the solver directly: you SOLVE. Crapulent means drunk or hungover.
explanation.definitionFit: Insolvent means unable to pay one's debts, which is what bankrupt means.

clue.text: You shouldn’t have clipped sea monkey

indicators.note: a clipped word has had its end cut off

blocks.note: said on receiving a gift; ta is British slang for thanks
MARINE, meaning of the sea, with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: A polite protest on being handed a strange gift: a sea monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: "Sea monkey" looks like one creature, but sea belongs to the wordplay. TA is British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A tamarin is a small South American monkey.

clue.text: Tory no more whose time has passed

definitions.note: the definition describes a person (one whose time has passed) rather than naming one

explanation.surface: A former Conservative whose political moment is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The words appear as CON then EX in the clue, but the answer puts EX first. "Time" is prison time: an ex-con has served it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ex-con is a former convict, someone whose prison time is behind them.

clue.text: Frau converted, absorbed in additional prayer

indicators.note: converted letters are changed into a new arrangement
the rearranged letters are taken inside another word

blocks.note: other = additional, as in other reasons

explanation.surface: A German woman who has converted to a new faith and is absorbed in extra prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: O(URFA)THER. Frau, the German for a married woman, is only letters here; "converted" suits the religious surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Our Father is the Lord's Prayer, named from its opening words.

clue.text: Measure pain after leaving hospital

indicators.note: what remains once H has left the word

blocks.note: H = hospital, as on road signs; it is removed

explanation.surface: Assessing how much pain a patient is in when discharged from hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: "Measure pain" reads as a nurse's task, but Measure is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ell is an old measure of length, used for cloth.

clue.text: Backed augury one found in movie?

indicators.note: the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A backed prophecy and someone turning up in a film.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful nod to the film title Finding Nemo: he is the one found in that movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemo is the clownfish who is found in the animated film Finding Nemo.

clue.text: Cécile is dancing with Mr D?

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman called Cécile dancing with a mysterious partner, Mr D.
explanation.walkthrough: "Mr D" reads as a man's name, but D stands alone as the definition: the capital letter is shaped like a half circle. The question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A capital D is a straight line closed by a semicircular curve, so D can suggest a semicircle.

clue.text: One attacking a crew member reported

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the answer sounds like the phrase

blocks.note: a sailor is a member of a ship's crew

explanation.surface: A news report that one of a ship's crew has been attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech "a sailor" and assailer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain agent noun: to assail is to attack, and the -er ending makes the person doing it.

clue.text: Tight times just around the corner

blocks.note: times as in multiplication: two by three

explanation.surface: Hard financial times are coming soon.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tight times" reads as austerity; tight means mean with money, which NEAR also means in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nearby is close at hand, just around the corner.

clue.text: Dear Welsh leopard destroyed residence

indicators.note: destroyed letters are broken up and put back in a new order

blocks.note: bach is a Welsh term of endearment, like dear

explanation.surface: A Welsh home wrecked by a leopard.
explanation.walkthrough: "Dear Welsh" reads like a letter opening; bach is the Welsh endearment, used much like dear or love.
explanation.definitionFit: A bachelor pad is a flat or house where a single man lives, a residence.

clue.text: High-street trader avoiding alcohol daily

blocks.note: a daily is a British term for a cleaner who comes each day

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper on the high street who has gone teetotal every day.
explanation.walkthrough: "Daily" looks like an adverb; in British English a daily is a domestic cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry-cleaner runs a shop, usually on the high street, cleaning clothes.

clue.text: Firms criticise one blocking move towards south

indicators.note: the pieces block the way by sitting inside another word

explanation.surface: Businesses criticising someone who is blocking a relocation to the south.
explanation.walkthrough: "Move towards south" looks like a relocation, but it is two separate pieces, with the criticism and the one lodged inside the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the commercial sense, the plural matching the plural definition.

clue.text: Agent to slow insect devouring pitch

indicators.note: the insect eats the pitch, taking it inside

explanation.surface: A pesticide wanted to slow down an insect that is chewing up the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: RE(TAR)DANT. The insect must be the specific RED ANT, not just ANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A retardant is a substance, an agent, that slows a process such as burning.

clue.text: Rhine wine or pop?

blocks.note: the British name for German white wine from the Rhine, from the town of Hochheim
to pop is British slang for to pawn, as in pop your watch

explanation.surface: A choice of drinks: German wine or a fizzy soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pop" poses as fizzy drink beside the wine, but it is the verb to pawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Hock is German Rhine wine; to hock something is to pawn it, to pop it.

clue.text: Goethe for one discarding an original thought

indicators.note: to discard is to throw away, as with a card from a hand, so AN is thrown out of the word

blocks.note: Goethe is an example of a German

explanation.surface: The poet Goethe abandoning an early idea.
explanation.walkthrough: "Original" here means first, starting: the germ of an idea is its seed.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ is the seed or starting point of an idea, an original thought.

clue.text: Sons leaving to track bird and rabbit directly

indicators.note: the sons walk out of the word, so the S that stands for them goes

blocks.note: STALK = track, with S for sons removed

explanation.surface: Hunters leave to stalk a game bird and a rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rabbit" is British slang for chatter or talk, so rabbit directly means speak frankly; the hunting surface hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk turkey is to speak plainly and frankly about a matter.

clue.text: Beat with undesirable acceleration in dance

blocks.note: a is the symbol for acceleration in physics

explanation.surface: A dancer finding the beat but speeding up in an unwelcome way.
explanation.walkthrough: "Beat" and "acceleration" feel musical, but they are LAM and the physics symbol A.
explanation.definitionFit: The lambada is a fast Brazilian partner dance.

clue.text: Really popular female performance

explanation.surface: Praise for a woman's performance that was very well received.
explanation.walkthrough: "Really" looks like an intensifier for popular; it is the definition standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sentence adverbs used to insist on the truth, as in 'really, it was' and 'in fact, it was'.

clue.text: Motorist finally learned to put foot down

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the word's end, its last letter, is used

blocks.note: to read a subject is to learn it, as in reading law

explanation.surface: A driver at last learns to press the accelerator.
explanation.walkthrough: "Put foot down" suggests accelerating in a car; here it is simply stepping.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for stepping, as in treading on a toe; the motoring sense of the phrase is the surface's decoy.

clue.text: Old woman hot in desert run

indicators.note: hot is placed in desert, read literally: one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: ma = mother, an old woman in slang

explanation.surface: An elderly woman sweltering as she runs through a desert.
explanation.walkthrough: MA then RAT(H)ON. "Desert" wants to be sand; it is the verb, to rat on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the marathon is the classic long-distance road race of 26.2 miles.

clue.text: Host hasn’t run very small outfit

indicators.note: the word does not have R, so R is removed

blocks.note: a host is a large crowd, a throng
R = run, as in cricket scores; it is removed

explanation.surface: A party host who hasn't run up anything bigger than a tiny outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: "Host" suggests a person throwing a party; here it is a multitude, as in a host of angels.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful understatement: a G-string barely counts as an outfit at all, hence very small.

clue.text: Wants facts about English team heading for relegation

indicators.note: the facts go around the other pieces
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A demand for the facts on an English football team facing relegation.
explanation.walkthrough: D(E SIDE R)ATA. Relegation is the drop to a lower division in British football leagues.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiderata are things wanted or needed, wants.

clue.text: Purpose Kennedy periodically reveals

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of kEnNeDy

explanation.surface: A Kennedy disclosing their aim from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of Kennedy spell END.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of goal, as in 'the ends justify the means'.

clue.text: Surgical procedure breaks bone: my mistake!

indicators.note: the operation breaks into the bone, sitting inside it

blocks.note: os is the Latin for bone, used in anatomy

explanation.surface: A surgeon breaking a bone during an operation and apologising.
explanation.walkthrough: O(OP)S. The surface reads as a surgeon's confession, which is exactly when you would say the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Oops is what you say to admit a small blunder: my mistake!

clue.text: Poor dealt with for fencing blue Aston Martin?

indicators.note: fencing encloses, so the outer word surrounds the others

blocks.note: to do something is to deal with it
the Vantage is a model of Aston Martin car

explanation.surface: Someone badly treated for putting a fence around a blue sports car.
explanation.walkthrough: DI(SAD VANTAGE)D. The question mark shows Aston Martin stands for one model of the car, the Vantage.
explanation.definitionFit: Disadvantaged means lacking resources or opportunities, poor.
